title: Current, potential difference and resistance
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Physics (8463) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.2.1-c10, 4.2.1-c23, 4.2.1-c04, 4.2.1-c11. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Resistance
items.clue: The opposition of a component to the flow of charge.

items.label: Light-dependent resistor (LDR)
items.clue: Conducts better in bright conditions than in the dark; used as a sensor.

items.label: Electric current
items.clue: A flow of charge; its size is how much charge passes a point each second.

items.label: Potential difference (pd)
items.clue: What drives charge round a circuit; measured across a component, in volts.

questions.stem: A resistor in a circuit is replaced by one of greater resistance, and the potential difference across it is unchanged. What happens to the current through it?

options.text: it stays the same, because the cell always pushes out the same current
it stays the same, because the pd across the component is unchanged
it stays the same, because the cell alone decides the current
it decreases, because a greater resistance opposes the flow of charge

questions.explanation: The greater the resistance of the component, the smaller the current for a given pd across it, which is I = V ÷ R.

questions.stem: Which statement about the resistance of circuit components is correct?

options.text: R is a fixed property of every component, in the way that mass is fixed
R never changes, not even in a thermistor or an LDR
for some components R is constant, in others it changes with current
R only changes in components built to sense their surroundings

questions.explanation: Exactly the distinction the specification draws: the value of R remains constant for some resistors but can change as the current changes in others.

questions.stem: A potential difference of 6.0 V across a component produces a current of 0.25 A through it. Calculate the resistance of the component.
questions.explanation: Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I = 6.0 ÷ 0.25 = 24 Ω, with resistance in ohms, Ω.

questions.stem: The I–V graph for a resistor at constant temperature is a straight line passing through the origin. What does this show?

options.text: the resistance rises steadily as the potential difference is increased
the resistance is equal to the gradient of the line at every point
the current does not depend on the resistor, since the cell fixes it
the current is directly proportional to the pd, so the resistance is constant

questions.explanation: A straight line through the origin is what direct proportionality looks like, and it means R remains constant as the current changes.

questions.stem: A resistor of resistance 15 Ω has a potential difference of 3.0 V across it. Calculate the current through the resistor.
questions.explanation: Rearranging V = I R gives I = V ÷ R = 3.0 ÷ 15 = 0.20 A, with current in amperes, A.

questions.stem: As the current through a filament lamp increases, what happens to the resistance of the lamp, and why?

options.text: it increases, because the filament becomes hotter
it stays constant, because the lamp is an ohmic conductor
it stays constant, because its I–V graph passes through the origin
it increases, because a bigger current always raises resistance

questions.explanation: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases, and a larger current heats it more.

questions.stem: In Required practical activity 3 a student doubles the length of nichrome wire in the circuit while keeping its temperature constant. What happens to the resistance of the wire?

options.text: it halves, because a longer wire gives the charge more room to move in
it is unchanged, since resistance depends only on the metal in use
it doubles, because resistance is proportional to the wire length
it falls to a quarter, because the longer wire gives even more room

questions.explanation: At constant temperature the resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length, so twice the length gives twice the resistance.

questions.stem: A diode is connected into a circuit the reverse way round. What is the current through it?

options.text: a tiny current, because the diode still leaks a little in reverse
almost zero, because the diode has a very high resistance in reverse
much smaller than the forward current, but still easy to measure
the same size as before, but now flowing the other way round

questions.explanation: The current through a diode flows in one direction only, because the diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.

questions.stem: A second resistor, identical to the first, is connected in parallel with it. What happens to the total resistance of the combination?

options.text: it doubles, because two resistors must resist more than one of them
it stays the same, since both resistors have the same resistance
it doubles, because the length of resistance wire has doubled
it halves, because the charge now has two separate paths to flow along

questions.explanation: A parallel branch gives the charge an extra route, so the combined resistance is smaller than either resistor alone — here exactly half.

questions.stem: A thermistor is taken out of a beaker of iced water and placed in a beaker of hot water. What happens to its resistance?

options.text: it increases, because heating any conductor raises its resistance
it stays the same, because resistance depends on the material only
it decreases, since a thermistor's resistance falls as it warms
it increases, because the warmer thermistor resists the current more

questions.explanation: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases, which is what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.

questions.stem: In Required practical activity 3 a student wants to find the resistance of a length of wire. Which pair of measurements is needed?

options.text: the pd across the wire and the current in it
readings from a voltmeter in the loop and an ammeter
the pd across the wire and the charge that flows in it
the pd across the wire and the length of the wire

questions.explanation: The ammeter gives I and the voltmeter gives V, and the resistance follows from R = V ÷ I.

questions.stem: A thermistor is used in a thermostat that switches a heater on when a room becomes too cold. What happens in the circuit as the room cools?

options.text: the thermistor's resistance falls, letting a larger current switch it on
the thermistor's resistance falls, so the heater stays switched off
the thermistor's resistance is unchanged, but the pd across it rises
the thermistor's resistance rises, and the circuit then switches the heater on

questions.explanation: Resistance falls as temperature rises, so cooling raises it; the switching circuit responds to that rise by turning the heater on.
